title: Promoting People Before They Are Ready
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article draws a sharp distinction between stretching people through challenging assignments — which the author endorses — and over-promoting them into roles they aren't ready for, which it warns against as a common and costly mistake. It reasons that failure at a project carries limited downside, but incompetence in an ongoing role can permanently damage a career and erode team trust. The piece offers a checklist of readiness questions leaders should run through before promoting someone, covering foundational skill, judgment, adaptability, and whether colleagues will actively support the promotion. The core lesson: stretch people through projects, not through premature title changes.
points: Failure at a stretch assignment is low-cost and reversible; failure in a promoted role is often career-damaging and hard to recover from.
A pre-promotion checklist — foundational skills, peer support, judgment, adaptability, receptiveness to feedback — is a practical gate against over-promotion.
The recommended fix isn't withholding challenge but channeling it: develop people through assignments and projects rather than through expanded formal roles.
quotes: There is an enormous difference between failing at an assignment and underperforming in a position or role.
There is a fine line between believing in people and giving them opportunities that will stretch them and promoting them before they are ready.
Team members and junior leaders who are promoted before they are ready can destroy team morale, team productivity, and team dynamics.
While leadership experts delight in pointing out the many benefits of failing, doing so in a new role or position can create permanent scarring.
The best leaders promote others when they are ready, not when they are available and willing.
